lessons.title: Case Study: Backtesting a Regime-Switching System on Nifty 50, 2015 to 2024

body.text: This case study runs the complete rigorous pipeline end to end: walk-forward fitting, a genuine untouched holdout, lag-aware evaluation, and an honest side-by-side comparison against the naive, leaky version this chapter has been warning about since Lesson 1.

children.text: Every warning in this chapter gets tested together here, on a full decade of Nifty 50 data: does avoiding look-ahead bias, measuring lag honestly, and holding out a genuine out-of-sample period change the headline number as much as this chapter has argued it should?

body.caption: A deliberate 7-year tuning window and a genuinely untouched 3-year holdout

cells: Hyperparameter search (K, refit frequency, self-transition prior), evaluated via walk-forward validation within this window only
Completely untouched during tuning; run exactly once, after every choice was finalized

children.text: The holdout period is not a convenient, easy stretch. It contains the entire 2022 rate-hike chop that broke Chapter 1's simple crossover system, followed by the 2023 to 2024 recovery, a genuinely mixed, non-trivial test.
Naive vs Rigorous, Side by Side

body.caption: The same underlying strategy, evaluated three different ways (illustrative)

body.text: Every number in this table is a hand-built illustration consistent with the direction and rough magnitude this chapter has argued for, not the output of an actual model run on real data. Build and run the real version yourself using Lesson 2's walk-forward loop before trusting any specific number.

Two separate gaps are visible here, and they mean different things. The gap from 2.7 (naive) to 1.1 (rigorous training) is roughly the size of the look-ahead and selection bias this entire chapter has been warning about, an illegitimate gap that should never have been there. The smaller gap from 1.1 (training) to 0.7 (holdout) is a normal, expected kind of degradation, the honest cost of testing on data the strategy genuinely never saw during tuning. Confusing these two gaps, treating all out-of-sample decay as equally alarming, or all of it as equally acceptable, misses the entire point of building the distinction this carefully.

children.text: Is a Holdout Sharpe of 0.7 Good or Bad?

0.7 is not spectacular. It is a modest, plausible Sharpe ratio for a systematic strategy after realistic costs, the kind of number that would not make headlines but could genuinely be worth trading. What makes it meaningful here is where it was earned: this holdout period is the exact 2022 stretch that broke Chapter 1's original crossover system, ending that year down roughly 13.4% on identical starting conditions.

body.label: Full circle: the same period, two very different outcomes
body.value: Chapter 1's crossover system: -13.4% in 2022. This case study's holdout: Sharpe 0.7, cumulative return approximately +20% over 2022 to 2024 (illustrative)
body.context: This is not proof of a durable edge, that requires real data and real trading. It is evidence that a regime-aware system, evaluated with the exact honesty this chapter insists on, can behave meaningfully differently in the regime that broke the course's very first example.

children.text: What This Case Study Does and Doesn't Prove

Every number in this lesson was hand-built to be directionally realistic, not measured. This case study does not prove that this specific regime-switching framework has genuine edge in real markets; only a real implementation, run on real data with real costs, could do that. What it does demonstrate is the methodology itself: the gap between a naive backtest and a rigorous one is not a minor technical footnote, it can be the entire difference between a strategy that looks like a career-making discovery and one that is honestly, modestly tradeable, or not tradeable at all. Carry the discipline forward, not any specific Sharpe ratio from this lesson.

body.title: Reading the Two Gaps Correctly
body.question: In this lesson's table, which gap represents an illegitimate result that should never have been reported, and which represents normal, expected degradation?
options: Both gaps are equally illegitimate and indicate the strategy has no value

The gap from 2.7 to 1.1 (naive to rigorous training) is the illegitimate one, reflecting look-ahead and selection bias; the smaller gap from 1.1 to 0.7 (training to holdout) is normal, expected out-of-sample decay
The gap from 1.1 to 0.7 is illegitimate; the gap from 2.7 to 1.1 is normal and expected
Neither gap matters as long as the final holdout Sharpe ratio is positive
body.explanation: The 2.7-to-1.1 gap is the direct cost of the failures Lessons 1 and 4 warned about, information the naive version had no legitimate right to. The 1.1-to-0.7 gap is the honest cost of testing on genuinely unseen data, a normal, expected form of decay that any real strategy should show to some degree, and its absence would itself be a warning sign of a holdout that was not truly untouched.

body.title: A Final Backtest Rigor Checklist
steps: Confirm every trading signal came from filtered probabilities generated by a walk-forward loop, never from a single full-sample fit's smoothed or Viterbi output (Lesson 1)
Confirm the walk-forward loop's slicing boundary strictly excludes any data beyond each point in time, and note the refit frequency and staleness tradeoff chosen (Lesson 2)
Measure and report the strategy's actual detection lag against at least one known historical regime shift, not an assumed or hoped-for lag (Lesson 3)
Disclose how many hyperparameter combinations were searched, and report a genuinely untouched holdout period's performance, run only once, alongside the tuning-period result (Lesson 4)

Report both the naive-to-rigorous gap and the training-to-holdout gap separately, and be able to explain what each one means, rather than presenting a single headline Sharpe ratio without this context

points: A deliberate 2015-2021 tuning period and a completely untouched 2022-2024 holdout let this case study separate look-ahead and selection bias from normal out-of-sample decay
In this illustrative comparison, the naive full-sample Sharpe ratio (2.7) fell to 1.1 on rigorous walk-forward evaluation within the training period, and to 0.7 on the untouched holdout
The gap from naive to rigorous reflects illegitimate bias this chapter warned about directly; the smaller gap from training to holdout reflects normal, expected degradation on genuinely unseen data
The holdout period covers the exact 2022 stretch that broke Chapter 1's original crossover system, giving this case study a meaningful full-circle test rather than a convenient one
This case study demonstrates a methodology, not a proven edge; the discipline built across this chapter is the actual takeaway to carry into Chapter 8's risk management
